mainTopic: רב יהודה's three 'lengthenings,' further lists of three, teachings about בצלאל and wisdom, and the nature of dreams.
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining רב יהודה's three kinds of 'lengthening' that bring long life. A long תפלה is good as long as the person does not expect an answer as his due; he lengthens it by adding pleas for mercy. A long meal is good because a poor person may come and be fed, and today a person's שלחן atones like the מזבח once did. Staying long in the בית הכסא is healthy only without straining, as the story of רבי יהודה ברבי אלעאי shows. Next come more lists of three: things that shorten life, things that need prayer (a good king, a good year, a good dream), and things ה׳ announces Himself. The mention of בצלאל as a good leader leads to several teachings. A leader must be approved by the community. בצלאל was named for his wisdom ('בצל אל'), and he knew the letters of creation. ה׳ gives wisdom only to the wise. The amud ends with a series of teachings about dreams from רב חסדא and others: every dream has some nonsense in it, and no dream comes true completely. The proof from יוסף's dream is explained on the next amud.

steps.title: A source says long prayer leads to heartache
steps.stepSummary: The challenge against רב יהודה continues. It quotes a teaching that one who prolongs his תפלה and expects an answer will end up heartbroken.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anyone who makes his prayer long and expects it to be answered will end up with heartache, as the verse says: 'Hope that is drawn out makes the heart sick.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a source that seems to contradict רב יהודה, who praised making one's תפלה long.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה said a long תפלה lengthens life. This source says a long תפלה paired with expectation (מעיין בה) leads to disappointment. The proof is the פסוק in משלי about drawn-out hope making the heart sick.

keyTerms.meaning: expects it to be answered; counts on it

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the word ומעיין בה. This source does not criticize a long תפלה by itself. It criticizes a long תפלה combined with expecting an answer. The תירוץ in step 3 depends on this detail.

phrases.english: Anyone who prolongs his prayer
and expects it to be answered —
will ultimately come to heartache,
as it is said: 'Hope deferred makes the heart sick.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge to רב יהודה's praise of a long תפלה, which began on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's statement that one who prolongs his תפלה has his days lengthened.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a long תפלה brings heartache, how can it be a cause of long life?

steps.title: A second source: expecting prayer to be answered calls up one's sins
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק lists three things that cause a person's sins to be remembered. One of them is עיון תפלה, expecting one's prayer to be answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: Three things bring up a person's sins: a leaning wall, expecting one's prayer to be answered, and handing a judgment against one's fellow over to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second source to strengthen the challenge against long תפלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item on רבי יצחק's list makes Heaven examine a person's record. A person standing by a leaning wall relies on a miracle. A person expecting his prayer to be answered claims he deserves it. A person asking Heaven to judge his fellow invites a comparison with himself. Since עיון תפלה is on the list, it strengthens the challenge against long prayer.

keyTerms.meaning: cause his sins to be remembered
a leaning wall about to fall
expecting one's prayer to be answered
handing over a case against one's fellow (to Heaven)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים מַזְכִּירִים עֲוֹנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם,
phrases.english: Three things call to mind a person's sins,
and they are: a leaning wall,
expecting prayer to be answered,
and handing over judgment of one's fellow to Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second source backing up the challenge from step 1.
steps.raayaObject: The challenge that a long תפלה is harmful rather than good.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יצחק's list, which includes עיון תפלה as something that calls up a person's sins.

steps.title: The difference is whether he expects an answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles the contradiction. The sources that criticize long prayer speak of someone who expects an answer. רב יהודה speaks of someone who does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This source is about someone who expects his prayer to be answered. That one is about someone who does not expect it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the sources are talking about two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A long תפלה itself is good, and it lengthens life, as רב יהודה said. The harm comes only from the attitude of expectation (עיון). If a person prays at length without feeling entitled to an answer, there is no problem.

keyTerms.meaning: this case... that case... (splitting two sources)

steps.whatToRemember: A long תפלה is praiseworthy. Expecting an answer because of it is what causes harm.

phrases.english: This is not difficult:
this is where he expects it to be answered,
that is where he does not expect it to be answered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in steps 1 and 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the sources describe different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every long תפלה is harmful and calls up one's sins.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a long תפלה with expectation is harmful. Without expectation, it lengthens life.

steps.title: How does he make his prayer long?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a long תפלה actually looks like in practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does he do it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short practical question to set up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that a long תפלה is approved, we need to know what makes a prayer 'long' in the good way.

keyTerms.meaning: and how does he do it?

phrases.english: And how does he do it? —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up question on the approved long תפלה from step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical way to lengthen one's תפלה.

steps.title: By adding more pleas for mercy
steps.stepSummary: He lengthens his prayer by adding more requests for mercy.
steps.simpleTranslation: He adds more pleas for mercy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a good long prayer means adding more begging for mercy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding רחמים fits the attitude of someone who is not counting on an answer. He keeps asking, as someone who knows he does not deserve it.

phrases.english: By increasing his pleas for mercy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He lengthens his תפלה by increasing his supplication.

steps.title: Why a long meal is good: a poor person may come
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the second item of רב יהודה. Lingering at the table gives a poor person a chance to arrive and be fed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who lingers at his table: perhaps a poor person will come, and he will give him food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second thing רב יהודה praised and explains the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Staying longer at the meal is not about eating more. It keeps food ready on the table, so a poor person who comes can be fed right away without waiting.

phrases.english: And one who lingers at his table:
perhaps a poor person will come
and he will give him food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first item of רב יהודה (תפלה) to the second item (the שלחן).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A long meal is praiseworthy because it gives the poor a chance to be fed.

steps.title: A verse that starts with the altar and ends with the table
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a פסוק in יחזקאל that describes a wooden מזבח and then calls it 'the table before ה׳'. It points out that this wording is strange.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'The altar of wood, three cubits high,' and it is written: 'And he said to me: This is the table that is before ה׳.' The verse began with the altar and ended with the table!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a verse to support the value of one's table, first noting that its wording is puzzling. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same object is called a מזבח at the start of the verse and a שלחן at the end. That change in wording needs an explanation, and the explanation is what connects a person's table to the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: it opened with... and ended with...

phrases.english: As it is written: 'The altar of wood, three cubits high,'
and it is written: 'And he said to me:
This is the table that is before the Lord,'
it opened with an altar and ended with a table!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a verse to back up the value of the table described in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: The importance of a person's שלחן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: יחזקאל מא:כב, which shifts from 'altar' to 'table'.

steps.title: Today a person's table atones like the altar
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר explain the verse. While the בית המקדש stood, the מזבח atoned. Now, a person's table atones for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר both say: As long as the בית המקדש stood, the altar atoned for Israel. Now, a person's table atones for him.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים explain the odd wording of the verse, and that explanation shows how great a person's table is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse calls the מזבח a שלחן to hint that a table can take over the altar's job. Feeding guests and the poor at one's table brings כפרה today, the way קרבנות did. This is why lingering at the table is so valuable.
steps.whatToRemember: After the חורבן, a person's שלחן, especially when used to feed the poor, takes the place of the מזבח in bringing כפרה.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both say:
As long as the Temple stood —
the altar atoned for Israel,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַכְשָׁיו, שֻׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מְכַפֵּר עָלָיו.
phrases.english: and now, a person's table atones for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the textual puzzle from step 7 and completes the support for step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Interpretive: the change in wording carries a message.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verse's switch from מזבח to שלחן is unexplained.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse teaches that a person's table now atones, as the מזבח once did.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching is the source for treating one's table like a מזבח, which underlies many מנהגים of the meal, such as feeding guests and the poor.

steps.title: Is staying long in the bathroom really a good thing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to רב יהודה's third item and questions whether lingering in the בית הכסא is a virtue.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who lingers in the bathroom: is that a virtue?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the third thing רב יהודה praised. Its proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling it 'a virtue' (מעליותא) is questioned because a source suggests it is actually harmful. This line opens the challenge, and the ברייתא in step 10 supplies the evidence.

phrases.english: And one who lingers in the bathroom:
is that a virtue?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the third item of רב יהודה's list.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's claim that lingering in the בית הכסא lengthens life.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Lingering in the bathroom seems harmful, so how can it be praised as lengthening life?

steps.title: The ברייתא of ten things that cause hemorrhoids
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists ten things that cause hemorrhoids. The last one, according to יש אומרים, is staying too long in the בית הכסא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: Ten things bring a person to hemorrhoids: eating reed leaves, grape leaves, grapevine tendrils, the rough palate of an animal, the spine of a fish, salted fish not fully cooked; drinking wine dregs; wiping with lime or clay; wiping with a stone that another person already used. And some say: also one who sits too long in the bathroom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא as proof for its challenge. It still needs an answer, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most items on the list are rough foods or harmful ways of wiping. The final opinion (יש אומרים) adds lingering too long in the בית הכסא. That item directly contradicts רב יהודה's praise.
steps.confusionAlert: Only the יש אומרים at the end of the list says that lingering is harmful. The words יותר מדאי ('too much') will matter when the גמרא answers.

phrases.english: But was it not taught:
Ten things bring a person
to hemorrhoids:
one who eats leaves of reeds,
grape leaves, and grapevine tendrils,
the rough palate of an animal, and the spine of a fish,

phrases.aramaic: וְדָג מָלִיחַ שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְבוּשָּׁל כׇּל צָרְכּוֹ,
phrases.english: and salted fish that is not fully cooked,
and one who drinks wine dregs,
and one who wipes himself with lime or clay.
And one who wipes with a stone that his fellow already wiped with,
and some say: also one who suspends himself
in the bathroom too long.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: עֲשָׂרָה דְּבָרִים מְבִיאִין אֶת הָאָדָם לִידֵי תַּחְתּוֹנִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the challenge raised in step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The challenge that lingering in the בית הכסא is harmful, not a virtue.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of ten causes of hemorrhoids, ending with 'one who suspends himself in the bathroom too long'.

steps.title: Two kinds of lingering: with straining and without
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא (harmful) is talking about someone who lingers and strains. רב יהודה (beneficial) is talking about someone who lingers without straining.
steps.simpleTranslation: No difficulty. The ברייתא means one who stays long and strains. רב יהודה means one who stays long and does not strain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from Step 10 by splitting the case into two situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources talk about staying long in the בית הכסא, but they describe different behavior. Staying long while straining or 'hanging' causes hemorrhoids, which is the ברייתא's case. Staying long calmly, without straining, is healthy, which is רב יהודה's case. So the two sources never disagreed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult: a standard opening for an answer

steps.whatToRemember: Lingering is fine. Straining is what causes harm.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this (the ברייתא) is where he stays long and strains,
phrases.notes: This is the case where it's harmful.

phrases.english: this (רב יהודה) is where he stays long and does not strain.
phrases.notes: This is the case where it's good for you.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דְּמַאֲרִיךְ וְתָלֵי, הָא דְּמַאֲרִיךְ וְלָא תָּלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised by the ברייתא in Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two sources describe different situations
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any lingering in the בית הכסא causes hemorrhoids, which contradicts רב יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only lingering with straining is harmful. Calm lingering is healthy.

steps.title: The matron and the healthy face of רבי יהודה ברבי אלעאי
steps.stepSummary: A matron mocked רבי יהודה ברבי אלעאי's healthy face. He explained that it came from relieving himself often on his way to the בית מדרש.
steps.simpleTranslation: A noblewoman said to רבי יהודה ברבי אלעאי: your face looks like that of pig farmers and lenders who take interest. He answered: honestly, both of those are forbidden to me. Rather, there are 24 bathrooms between my lodging and the בית מדרש, and when I walk I check myself in every one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows how good it is for health to take care of one's bodily needs properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The matron hinted that his round, healthy face must come from an easy, dishonest income. He answered that both jobs are forbidden to a Jew. His good health came from never holding in his needs, which supports רב יהודה's praise of taking one's time there.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דַּאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ הָהִיא מַטְרוֹנִיתָא
phrases.english: Like that time when a certain matron said to
Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi El'ai:
Your face looks like that of pig farmers
phrases.notes: He means you look like someone with an easy, well-fed life.

phrases.english: and lenders who charge interest.
He said to her: Honestly,
for me, both of them are forbidden;
rather, twenty-four bathrooms
there are between my lodging and the study hall,
and when I walk,
I check myself in all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דַּאֲמַרָה לֵיהּ הָהִיא מַטְרוֹנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the healthy side of the answer in Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: Taking care of bodily needs without delay or straining is good for health.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי יהודה ברבי אלעאי and the matron.

steps.title: Three things that shorten a person's life
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה lists three behaviors that shorten life: refusing an עלייה to read the תורה, refusing to lead ברכת המזון over the כוס, and acting with superiority.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה also said: three things shorten a person's days and years. One who is given a ספר תורה to read and does not read. One who is given a כוס של ברכה to bless and does not bless. And one who acts like a lord over others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching of רב יהודה, another list of three. This opens a new topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two items are about turning down an honor connected to מצוות: reading the תורה and leading the blessing. The third is the opposite mistake, grabbing power and acting superior. The sources for each item come in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: The cup of wine over which ברכת המזון is led
One who acts with authority or superiority over others

steps.confusionAlert: Earlier, רב יהודה listed three things that LENGTHEN life. This is a different list, of three things that SHORTEN it.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים מְקַצְּרִים יָמָיו וּשְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם:
phrases.english: Three things shorten a person's days and years:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁנּוֹתְנִין לוֹ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה לִקְרוֹת
phrases.english: one who is given a Torah scroll to read
and he does not read;
a cup of blessing to bless over
and he does not bless;
and one who conducts himself with superiority.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים מְקַצְּרִים יָמָיו וּשְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching of רב יהודה that follows his earlier list of three.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Refusing to read the תורה, refusing to lead the blessing, and acting superior all shorten life.

steps.title: Sources for the ספר תורה and the כוס של ברכה
steps.stepSummary: The תורה is called 'your life and length of days', so refusing it shortens life. 'I will bless those who bless you' shows that refusing to bless loses blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Being given a ספר תורה and not reading: as it says, 'For it is your life and the length of your days.' Being given a כוס של ברכה and not blessing: as it says, 'I will bless those who bless you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a פסוק as the source for each of the first two items in רב יהודה's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה itself is the source of long life, so someone who turns down a chance to read it gives up that length of days. ה׳ blesses those who bless, so someone who turns down the chance to bless loses that blessing, which includes long life.

keyTerms.meaning: Your life and the length of your days
I will bless those who bless you

phrases.english: A Torah scroll to read and he does not read:
as it is written: 'For it is your life and the length of your days.'

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹס שֶׁל בְּרָכָה לְבָרֵךְ וְאֵינוֹ מְבָרֵךְ —
phrases.english: A cup of blessing to bless and he does not bless:
as it is written: 'I will bless those who bless you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה לִקְרוֹת וְאֵינוֹ קוֹרֵא, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the sources for the first two items in Step 13.
steps.raayaObject: Refusing to read the תורה or to bless shortens life.

steps.title: יוסף died first because he acted with authority
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא בר חנינא teaches that יוסף died before his brothers because he acted with superiority. This is the source for the third item.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who acts with superiority: as רבי חמא בר חנינא said, why did יוסף die before his brothers? Because he conducted himself with authority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the third item: the early death of יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'And יוסף died, and all his brothers' shows that יוסף died first, even though he was one of the younger brothers. רבי חמא בר חנינא explains that this was because he held a position of rule and authority. So leadership carried out with superiority shortens life.
steps.whatToRemember: Turning down a מצוה honor and acting superior to others both shorten a person's life. יוסף is the example for the danger of ruling over others.

phrases.english: And one who conducts himself with superiority:
as Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina said:

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה מֵת יוֹסֵף קוֹדֶם לְאֶחָיו —
phrases.english: Why did Joseph die before his brothers?
phrases.notes: Based on שמות א:ו, where יוסף's death is listed first

phrases.english: Because he conducted himself with superiority.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַמַּנְהִיג עַצְמוֹ בְּרַבָּנוּת — דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the third item in Step 13.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חמא בר חנינא's teaching on why יוסף died before his brothers.

steps.title: Three good things that require prayer
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says three things need רחמים: a good king, a good year, and a good dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Three things need prayer for mercy: a good king, a good year, and a good dream.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another three-part teaching from רב יהודה. This time it names three good things that we must pray for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that none of these three is fully in human control. Whether a king is good, a year is blessed, or a dream is positive depends on ה׳. So we must ask for them in prayer.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
Three things require prayer for mercy:

phrases.aramaic: מֶלֶךְ טוֹב, שָׁנָה טוֹבָה וַחֲלוֹם טוֹב.
phrases.english: a good king, a good year, and a good dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another three-item teaching from רב יהודה, following his list of three things that shorten life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A good king, a good year, and a good dream all require prayer.

steps.title: Verses for the three things that need prayer
steps.stepSummary: Each of the three items is supported by a פסוק showing that it is in ה׳'s hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: A good king, as it says: 'Like streams of water is the king's heart in ה׳'s hand.' A good year, as it says: 'ה׳ your God's eyes are always on it, from the beginning of the year to the end of the year.' A good dream, as it says: 'You will heal me (ותחלימני) and give me life.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse for each of the three items in רב יהודה's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The king's heart is 'in ה׳'s hand,' so a good king comes from Him. The year is under ה׳'s constant watch. The word ותחלימני sounds like חלום, so it is read as a request for good dreams.

keyTerms.meaning: You will heal me, read here as related to חֲלוֹם (dream)

steps.confusionAlert: The proof for a good dream is a wordplay. ותחלימני literally means 'heal me,' but the גמרא connects it to the word חלום.

phrases.english: A good king, as it is written:
"Like streams of water is the king's heart in the hand of the Lord."
A good year, as it is written:
"The eyes of the Lord your God are always upon it,
from the beginning of the year until the end of the year."
A good dream, as it is written:
"You will heal me (dream-related wording) and give me life."
phrases.notes: There's a wordplay here: תחלימני sounds like חלום, a dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides a source for each item listed in Step 16.
steps.raayaObject: That kings, years, and dreams depend on ה׳ and so require prayer.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי כא:א; דברים יא:יב; ישעיה לח:טז

steps.title: Three things ה׳ announces Himself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says הקדוש ברוך הוא personally proclaims famine, plenty, and a good leader.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: There are three things that הקדוש ברוך הוא announces Himself, and they are: famine, plenty, and a good leader.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a similar three-part teaching from רבי יוחנן. It lists three things that ה׳ Himself 'calls for.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: These three matters are so important for the community that ה׳ decrees them directly rather than through messengers. The third item, a good leader, sets up the discussion about בצלאל that follows.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Three things are proclaimed

phrases.aramaic: הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ וְאֵלּוּ הֵן:
phrases.english: by the Holy One, Blessed be He, Himself, and they are:
famine, plenty, and a good leader.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים מַכְרִיז עֲלֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel three-item list, linked thematically to the previous one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ personally proclaims famine, plenty, and a good leader.

steps.title: Verses showing ה׳ 'calls' for each
steps.stepSummary: Each item is supported by a פסוק using the word 'call' (קרא).
steps.simpleTranslation: Famine, as it says: 'For ה׳ has called for famine.' Plenty, as it says: 'I will call for the grain and increase it.' A good leader, as it says: 'ה׳ spoke to משה saying: See, I have called by name בצלאל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves each of רבי יוחנן's three items with a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The common thread is the root קרא, meaning 'call.' In each verse ה׳ Himself 'calls': for famine, for grain, and for בצלאל by name. That is the proof that ה׳ proclaims these things personally.

keyTerms.meaning: the chief builder of the מִשְׁכָּן

phrases.english: Famine, as it is written:
"For the Lord has called for a famine, etc."
Plenty, as it is written:
"And I will call for the grain and increase it."
A good leader, as it is written:
"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
See, I have called by name Bezalel, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the sources for Step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That ה׳ personally proclaims famine, plenty, and a good leader.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים ב ח:א; יחזקאל לו:כט; שמות לא:א-ב

steps.title: A leader must be approved by the community
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק rules that a פרנס may not be appointed over the community without consulting the community. He cites the verse about בצלאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: We do not appoint a leader over the community unless we consult the community, as it says: 'See, ה׳ has called by name בצלאל.'
steps.whatsHappening: Building on בצלאל as a 'good leader,' רבי יצחק states a practical rule about appointing communal leaders. He sets up a verse that the next step explains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse here is משה speaking to the people ('ראו', plural), not ה׳ speaking to משה. Telling the people 'see' shows that the people were brought into the decision.
steps.confusionAlert: This verse (ראו, plural) is different from the one in Step 19 (ראה, singular). The plural verse is addressed to the people, and that is why it proves consultation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical principle of Jewish communal leadership: leaders need the agreement of those they lead.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
One may not appoint a leader over the community
unless the community is consulted,
as it is stated: "See (plural), the Lord has called by name Bezalel."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אֵין מַעֲמִידִין פַּרְנָס עַל הַצִּבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Branches off from the mention of בצלאל as a good leader.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A communal leader may only be appointed after consulting the community.

steps.title: ה׳ asks משה, and משה asks the people
steps.stepSummary: A dialogue shows ה׳ consulting משה about בצלאל and then sending him to ask the people, even though everyone already agrees.
steps.simpleTranslation: ה׳ said to משה: 'משה, is בצלאל suitable in your eyes?' משה said: 'Master of the world, if he is suitable to You, surely he is suitable to me!' ה׳ said: 'Even so, go tell them.' משה went and asked ישראל: 'Is בצלאל suitable in your eyes?' They said: 'If he is suitable to ה׳ and to you, surely he is suitable to us!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells the story behind the verse, showing how the community was consulted about בצלאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when the answer was obvious, ה׳ insisted that the people be asked. That is the proof for רבי יצחק's rule: consultation is required, not just a formality you can skip when agreement is clear.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses:
Moses, is Bezalel suitable in your eyes?
He said to Him: Master of the universe,

phrases.aramaic: אִם לְפָנֶיךָ הָגוּן — לְפָנַי לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן!
phrases.english: if he is suitable before You, then all the more so before me!

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן, לֵךְ אֱמוֹר לָהֶם.
phrases.english: He said to him: Even so, go tell them.
He went and said to Israel:
Is Bezalel suitable in your eyes?

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אִם לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: They said to him: If before the Holy One, Blessed be He,

phrases.aramaic: וּלְפָנֶיךָ הוּא הָגוּן, לְפָנֵינוּ לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן!
phrases.english: and before you he is suitable, then all the more so before us!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה: מֹשֶׁה, הָגוּן עָלֶיךָ בְּצַלְאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the verse cited in Step 20 and shows how it proves the rule.
steps.raayaObject: That the community must be consulted before appointing a leader.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The דרשה on שמות לה:ל describing the consultation about בצלאל.
steps.whatToRemember: Even ה׳, who chose בצלאל, required that משה and the people be asked first. Consulting the community is required.

steps.title: בצלאל was named for his wisdom
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני in the name of רבי יונתן says the name בצלאל reflects his wisdom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: בצלאל was given his name because of his wisdom.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching about בצלאל begins. It explains his name and sets up a story that shows his wisdom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim is that the name itself hints at a special quality of בצלאל. The story that follows shows what that wisdom was and how the name fits it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan:
Bezalel was called by that name because of his wisdom.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues discussing בצלאל, now focusing on his name and wisdom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name בצלאל reflects his wisdom.

steps.title: משה reverses the order and בצלאל objects
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ commanded the order 'משכן, ארון, כלים.' משה told בצלאל the reverse order, and בצלאל logically argued that the building must come first.
steps.simpleTranslation: When ה׳ told משה, 'Go tell בצלאל: Make Me a משכן, an ארון, and vessels,' משה went and reversed it, telling him: 'Make an ארון, vessels, and a משכן.' בצלאל said: 'משה רבינו, the way of the world is that a person builds a house and then brings vessels into it. You say make an ארון, vessels, and a משכן. Where will I put the vessels I make? Perhaps ה׳ told you: Make a משכן, an ארון, and vessels?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story to prove בצלאל's wisdom. He figured out the correct order of building even though משה told it to him backwards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah lists the vessels first in one place (פרשת תרומה) and the משכן first in another (פרשת כי תשא). בצלאל reasoned from common sense that a house is built before its furniture. From that he correctly guessed what ה׳ had actually said.

keyTerms.meaning: the normal way of the world

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: When the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses:
Go say to Bezalel:
"Make Me a Tabernacle, an Ark, and vessels,"
Moses went, reversed it, and said to him:
"Make an Ark, vessels, and a Tabernacle."
He said to him: Moses our teacher,

phrases.aramaic: מִנְהָגוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם אָדָם בּוֹנֶה בַּיִת
phrases.english: the way of the world is that a person builds a house
and afterward brings vessels into it,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַתָּה אוֹמֵר ״עֲשֵׂה לִי אָרוֹן וְכֵלִים וּמִשְׁכָּן״,
phrases.english: yet you say: "Make me an Ark, vessels, and a Tabernacle."
The vessels that I make, where will I put them?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא כָּךְ אָמַר לְךָ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: Perhaps this is what the Holy One, Blessed be He, told you:
"Make a Tabernacle, an Ark, and vessels"?!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the story that demonstrates the wisdom claimed in Step 22.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the reversed order of building the משכן.

steps.title: משה's reply: were you in God's shadow?
steps.stepSummary: משה confirms בצלאל was right and connects his name to 'בצל אל,' meaning 'in God's shadow.'
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said to him: 'Perhaps you were in the shadow of God (בצל אל), and so you knew?'
steps.whatsHappening: משה admits that בצלאל guessed exactly what ה׳ said. This line wraps up the explanation of his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name בצלאל is split into בצל אל, 'in God's shadow.' בצלאל knew ה׳'s words as if he had been standing right there. This completes רבי יונתן's claim that the name reflects his wisdom.

keyTerms.meaning: in the shadow of God (wordplay on בְּצַלְאֵל)

steps.whatToRemember: בצלאל = בצל אל, 'in God's shadow.' His wisdom let him sense ה׳'s exact words, which is why he was the right leader to build the משכן.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: שֶׁמָּא בְּצֵל אֵל הָיִיתָ וְיָדַעְתָּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Perhaps you were in the shadow of God and knew?
phrases.notes: A play on the name בצלאל, read as בצל אל, 'in the shadow of God.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: שֶׁמָּא בְּצֵל אֵל הָיִיתָ וְיָדַעְתָּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: משה's response confirms בצלאל's reasoning and ties it to his name.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: בצלאל's name means 'in God's shadow,' reflecting his wisdom in knowing ה׳'s exact command.

steps.title: בצלאל knew the letters of creation
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that בצלאל knew how to combine the letters that heaven and earth were created with.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: בצלאל knew how to put together the letters that heaven and earth were created with.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more praise of בצלאל: he knew the 'letter-combinations' ה׳ used to create the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps showed that בצלאל was wise about the building order of the משכן. Here רב goes further and links his wisdom to the wisdom of creation itself. This suggests that building the משכן was like a small version of creating the world.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Bezalel knew
how to join letters
with which heaven and earth were created.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the praise of בצלאל's wisdom.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בצלאל knew the letter-combinations used to create heaven and earth.

steps.title: Proof from matching words of wisdom
steps.stepSummary: The same three words, wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, describe both בצלאל and the creation of the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, about בצלאל, it says: 'I filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge.' There, about creation, it says: 'ה׳ founded the earth with wisdom and set up the heavens with understanding,' and 'With His knowledge the depths split open.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רב's statement by showing that the verses use the same words for בצלאל and for creation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about בצלאל lists three qualities: חכמה, תבונה, and דעת. The verses in משלי use these same three qualities to describe how ה׳ created the world. So בצלאל had exactly the tools of creation.

keyTerms.meaning: it is written here, and it is written there (a comparison of two verses)

phrases.english: It is written here:
"And I filled him with the spirit of God,
in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge";
and it is written there:
"The Lord, by wisdom, founded the earth;
by understanding He established the heavens."
And it is written: "By His knowledge the depths were broken up."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the verse-proof for רב's statement.
steps.raayaObject: בצלאל knew the letters of creation.

steps.title: ה׳ gives wisdom only to the wise
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that ה׳ gives wisdom only to someone who already has wisdom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: ה׳ gives wisdom only to someone who already has wisdom, as the verse says: 'He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know understanding.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the גמרא was just discussing the wisdom ה׳ gave בצלאל, it brings a related teaching: ה׳ adds wisdom to people who are already wise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually we might expect wisdom to be given to someone who lacks it. רבי יוחנן says the opposite: wisdom builds on wisdom. His proof comes from the book of דניאל.

keyTerms.meaning: the Holy One, Blessed be He
He gives wisdom to the wise (Aramaic, from דניאל)

steps.confusionAlert: This verse is in Aramaic because it comes from the book of דניאל, not because the גמרא switched languages.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נוֹתֵן חָכְמָה
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not grant wisdom
except to one who has wisdom,
as it is stated: "He gives wisdom to the wise,
and knowledge to those who know understanding."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching about wisdom, connected to the topic of בצלאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ grants wisdom only to those who already have wisdom.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's different verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו agrees with the idea but learns it from a verse about the builders of the משכן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב תחליפא from ארץ ישראל heard this and repeated it before רבי אבהו. רבי אבהו said to him: You learn it from there, but we learn it from here, as it is written: 'And in the heart of everyone who is wise-hearted I placed wisdom.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו accepts רבי יוחנן's idea but brings a different source for it, a verse from the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no argument about the rule itself. Only the source changes, from דניאל to שמות. This also ties the idea back to the builders of the משכן, the same context as בצלאל.

keyTerms.meaning: from the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rav Taḥalifa from the West heard
and said it before Rabbi Abbahu.
He said to him:
You learn it from there;
we learn it from here,
as it is written: "And in the heart of all who are wise-hearted
I have placed wisdom."

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן מֵהָתָם מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ אֲנַן מֵהָכָא מַתְנִינַן לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative source for the same rule.
steps.raayaObject: ה׳ gives wisdom only to the wise.
steps.whatToRemember: ה׳ gives wisdom to people who already have it. רבי יוחנן learns this from דניאל, and רבי אבהו learns it from the verse about the builders of the משכן.

steps.title: Any dream except during a fast
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says any dream is acceptable, except a dream seen during a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Any dream is fine, but not one during a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: a list of sayings about dreams from רב חסדא. This is the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This short line means that any dream is better than a dream seen during a fast. רש״י explains that a dream seen while fasting is not a good one.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said:
Any dream, and not a fast.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new section of sayings about dreams.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any dream is preferable to a dream seen during a fast.

steps.title: An uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter
steps.stepSummary: A dream that is never interpreted has no effect, just like a letter that is never read.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: A dream that is not interpreted is like a letter that is not read.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא's second saying: a dream's meaning depends on its being interpreted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A letter carries a message, but until someone reads it, nothing happens. In the same way, the interpretation of a dream is what gives it its effect.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
A dream that is not interpreted
is like a letter that is not read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next saying in רב חסדא's series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream's interpretation is what activates it.

steps.title: No dream comes true completely
steps.stepSummary: Neither a good dream nor a bad dream is fulfilled in full.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: A good dream is not fully fulfilled, and a bad dream is not fully fulfilled.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא's third saying: dreams come true only in part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets the expectation that a dream is never a complete prediction. At the end of this section, רבי שמעון בן יוחאי gives the reason: every dream contains some nonsense.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
A good dream is not entirely fulfilled,
and a bad dream is not entirely fulfilled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next saying in the series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No dream, good or bad, is fulfilled in its entirety.

steps.title: A bad dream is better than a good one
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says a bad dream is preferable to a good dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: A bad dream is better than a good dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא's fourth saying, which sounds surprising: a bad dream is better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A bad dream frightens a person, and that fear moves him to do תשובה. A good dream can make a person feel too comfortable. So the spiritual result of a bad dream is better.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
A bad dream is preferable to a good dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next saying in the series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bad dream is preferable because it leads to תשובה.

steps.title: The feeling itself uses up the dream
steps.stepSummary: The sadness from a bad dream, or the joy from a good dream, can take the place of the dream actually happening.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: For a bad dream, the sadness it causes is enough. For a good dream, the joy it causes is enough.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא's fifth saying: the emotion a dream causes can count as its fulfillment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeling sad after a bad dream can replace the bad event itself, which is comforting. But the same works the other way: the joy of a good dream can 'use it up,' so it may not come true.

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
A bad dream: its sadness is enough for it;
a good dream: its joy is enough for it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next saying in the series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emotion caused by a dream can replace its actual fulfillment.

steps.title: רב יוסף: even for me, joy cancels a good dream
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף supports רב חסדא from his own experience: the joy of a good dream cancels it, even for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: A good dream, even for me, the joy it brings cancels it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף backs up רב חסדא's last saying with his own life experience.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף was blind and suffered a great deal, so you might expect a good dream to barely cheer him up. Yet even he felt so much joy from a good dream that it was 'used up' and never came true. This shows how strong the rule is.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
A good dream, even for me,
its joy negates it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the second half of step 33.
steps.raayaObject: The joy of a good dream can cancel its fulfillment.

steps.title: A bad dream is worse than lashes
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says a bad dream is harder than lashes, and proves it from a verse that רבי יוחנן explains as referring to a bad dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: A bad dream is harder than lashes, as it says: 'And God made it so that people would fear Him.' And רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This refers to a bad dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא's last saying: a bad dream hurts more than lashes. He brings a verse, and רבי יוחנן's explanation of that verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ uses a bad dream to make people fear Him, which shows how powerful its effect is. The verse alone does not mention dreams. רבי יוחנן's teaching that it means a bad dream is what completes the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: so that they will fear Him

phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said:
A bad dream is harder than lashes,
as it is stated: "And God has made it
so that they should fear before Him,"

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: and Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
This is a bad dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final saying in רב חסדא's series, with a verse-proof attached.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bad dream affects a person more strongly than lashes.
steps.whatToRemember: רב חסדא's dream rules: a dream works through its interpretation, no dream comes fully true, the feeling a dream causes can replace its fulfillment, and a bad dream is powerful and leads to fear of ה׳.

steps.title: What do straw and grain have to do with a dream?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a verse in ירמיהו that compares dreams to straw and grain, and asks what the connection is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'The prophet who has a dream, let him tell the dream; and whoever has My word, let him speak My word truthfully. What does the straw have to do with the grain? says ה׳.' What do grain and straw have to do with a dream?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a verse and asks a question about it. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse suddenly mentions straw and grain while discussing dreams, which seems out of place. The גמרא wants to know the link.

keyTerms.meaning: what does it have to do with

phrases.english: "The prophet who has a dream,
let him tell a dream;
and he who has My word,
let him speak My word truthfully.

phrases.aramaic: מַה לַתֶּבֶן אֶת הַבָּר נְאֻם ה׳״.
phrases.english: What has the straw to do with the grain? says the Lord."

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מָה עִנְיַן בַּר וְתֶבֶן אֵצֶל חֲלוֹם?
phrases.english: And what do grain and straw have to do with a dream?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מָה עִנְיַן בַּר וְתֶבֶן אֵצֶל חֲלוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the dream topic with a verse that needs explaining.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The connection between straw and grain and dreams.

steps.title: Every dream contains some nonsense
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן יוחאי explains that just as grain always grows with straw, every dream comes with some meaningless parts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי: Just as grain cannot grow without straw, a dream cannot exist without some meaningless things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the verse teaches that every dream, even a true one, has some nonsense mixed in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The grain stands for the true part of the dream, and the straw stands for the meaningless parts. This explains רב חסדא's earlier rule that no dream comes true completely: the 'straw' never comes true.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְבַר בְּלֹא תֶּבֶן,
phrases.english: Just as it is impossible for grain without straw,

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לַחֲלוֹם בְּלֹא דְּבָרִים בְּטֵלִים.
phrases.english: so too it is impossible for a dream without idle matters.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Straw and grain are a parable: every dream contains some idle content alongside the meaningful part.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the reason behind רב חסדא's rule (step 31) that no dream is fulfilled in its entirety.
steps.whatToRemember: Every dream, even a true one, has some nonsense mixed in, like straw that always comes with grain.

steps.title: Part of a dream may come true, but never all of it
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברכיה teaches that even when part of a dream is fulfilled, the entire dream is never fulfilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ברכיה said: A dream, even though part of it comes true, the whole of it does not come true.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא, רבי ברכיה, gives a short rule about dreams. Part of a dream can happen in real life, but never every detail of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the previous step, where רבי שמעון בן יוחאי said every dream has some meaningless 'straw' mixed in. רבי ברכיה draws the practical result: because of that extra material, a dream is never fulfilled 100%. The meaningful part can still come true.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole thing

steps.confusionAlert: רבי ברכיה is not saying that dreams don't come true. He is saying that part of a dream can come true, but never the whole dream.

phrases.english: Rabbi Berekhya said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲלוֹם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּקְצָתוֹ מִתְקַיֵּים —
phrases.english: A dream, even though part of it is fulfilled —
all of it is not fulfilled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבי שמעון בן יוחאי's 'straw and grain' idea and states its result: a dream is never completely fulfilled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream may be partially fulfilled, but it is never fulfilled in its entirety.

steps.title: Asking for the source of רבי ברכיה's rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that a dream is never completely fulfilled.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רבי ברכיה's rule. This is a setup line that prepares for the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא is not attacking רבי ברכיה. It simply wants to know which פסוק or story shows his rule to be true.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: From where do we derive this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule just stated in Step 38.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source showing that a dream comes true only in part.

steps.title: The source is יוסף's dream of the sun and the moon
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings יוסף's dream, where the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowed to him, as the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it from יוסף, as it is written: 'and behold, the sun and the moon, and so on.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to יוסף's second dream in ספר בראשית. It quotes only the opening words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In that dream the sun (יעקב), the moon (his mother רחל) and eleven stars (his brothers) bow down to יוסף. יעקב and the brothers did later bow to יוסף, so part of the dream came true. But רחל had already died, so the 'moon' part could never happen. That shows a dream comes true only in part, and the גמרא spells this out right on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Joseph, son of יעקב, who dreamed prophetic dreams
As it is written (introduces a פסוק)
The sun and the moon (symbols in יוסף's dream for his father and mother)
'Etc.', meaning the rest of the פסוק

steps.whatToRemember: רבי ברכיה: a dream can come true in part, but never completely. The proof is יוסף's dream. The 'moon' stood for רחל, who had already died, so that detail could not come true.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that even a real, prophetic dream like יוסף's still contained a detail that did not come true. That fits רבי שמעון בן יוחאי's rule that every dream has some 'straw' in it.

phrases.english: From Joseph, as it is written:
phrases.notes: יוסף's second dream, in בראשית chapter 37.

phrases.english: "And behold, the sun and the moon, etc."
phrases.notes: The full פסוק continues: 'and eleven stars were bowing down to me.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 39 by naming the source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יוסף's dream of the sun, the moon and the stars. It was fulfilled for his father and brothers but not for his mother, who had already died.
